extracted.intended_audience: general pop-culture readers and fans of celebrity roasts
extracted.subtask_description: A short popular-history overview of the origins, evolution, and broadcast adaptation of celebrity roasts from the Friars Club to modern TV/streaming revivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition: humorously insult the honoree
rubrics_metrics.description: "Celebrity roasts have become a form of popular entertainment, where famous stars come together to humorously insult one another—particularly the one being 'honored' with the gathering."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central feature of a roast is reciprocal, comedic insult directed especially at the event's honoree; tone is comedic and the insults are the primary entertainment vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and social setting (Friars Club/private dinners)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice grew out of early-to-mid 1900s gatherings of theater agents at the Friars Club; by 1949 the Friars Club made roasting a theme and formalized them as members and guest-only dinners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically roasts were private, membership/guest-only events often tied to social functions and fundraising (e.g., raising money for World War I veterans). This private setting influenced both content and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language register and broadcast suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The language used in these interactions was considered too vulgar for primetime television, so much of the original material remained private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because roasts historically involved vulgar language, adapting them for broadcast requires content moderation; however, selective clips were aired (e.g., Kraft Music Hall) before full TV adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television adaptation practice: minimize profanity for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When Dean Martin brought roasts to NBC in 1973, he made them more accessible TV entertainment "while keeping the profanity to a minimum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful televised roasts balance the edge of roast humor with broadcast standards — toning down profanity and vulgarity to reach wider audiences while preserving insult-based comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/participant expectations and tonal range
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts feature comedians and celebrities (examples: Don Rickles, Dean Martin, Joey Bishop) and can range from light-hearted to "unhinged"; not all participants take the session light-heartedly (e.g., Chevy Chase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a line-up of peers and comic performers trading jokes about the honoree; tone can vary and, historically, some roasts have been confrontational rather than purely affectionate. This affects how an audience perceives the event.
